title: Why we do not join the public festivals
source_text: Ἴδωμεν δὲ καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς Κέλσῳ λεγόμενα περὶ θεοῦ. καὶ ὡς προτρέπει ἡμᾶς ἐπὶ τὴν τῶν ὡς μὲν πρὸς ἀλήθειαν εἰδωλοθύτων χρῆσιν ἢ. ἵν᾿ οὕτως ὀνομάσω, δαιμονιοθύτων, ὡς δ᾿ αὐτὸς προσαγορεύσαι ἂν, ἅτε μὴ εἰδὼς, τί τὸ ἀληθῶς ἱερὸν, καὶ ποδαπαὶ αἱ παρὰ τούτῳ θυσίαι, ἱεροθύτων. ἃ δὲ λέγει, τοιαῦτά ἐστιν· ὅ γε μὴν θεὸς ἅπασι κοινὸς, ἀγαθός τε καὶ ἀπροσδεὴς καὶ ἔξω φθόνου· τί οὖν κωλύει τοὺς μάλιστα καθωσιωμένους αὐτῷ καὶ τῶν δημοτελῶν ἑορτῶν μεταλαμβάνειν; οὐκ οἶδα δὲ τί φαντασθεὶς οἴεται ἀκολουθεῖν τῷ τὸν θεὸν εἶναι ἀγαθὸν καὶ ἀπροσδεῆ καὶ ἔξω φθόνου τὸ τοὺς καθωσιωμένους αὐτῷ μεταλαμβάνειν τῶν δημοτελῶν ἑορτῶν. καί φημι ὅτι ἠκολούθει μὲν τῷ τὸν θεὸν εἶναι ἀγαθὸν καὶ ἀπροσδεῆ καὶ ἔξω φθόνου τὸ αὐτῶν τῶν δημοτελῶν μεταλαμβάνειν ἑορτῶν, εἰ ἀπεδείκνυτο ὅτι αἱ δημοτελεῖς ἑορταὶ οὐδὲν μὲν ἔχουσιν ἐσφαλμένον ἀπὸ δὲ τῆς περὶ θεοῦ θεωρίας ἐνομοθετήθησαν ὡς ἀκόλουθοι τῇ εἰς αὐτὸν θεραπείᾳ καὶ εὐσεβείᾳ. εἰ μέντοι αἱ δημοτελεῖς μέχρι ὀνόματος ἑορταὶ μηδένα λόγον ἔχουσιν ἀποδεικτικὸν, ὡς ἁρμόζουσαι τῇ εἰς τὸ θεῖον θεραπείᾳ, ἀλλ᾿ ἐλέγχοιντο οὖσαι ἀναπλάσματα τῶν ὅπως ποτὲ ἔτυχε διά τινας ἱστορίας ἀνθρωπικὰς ταῦτα νομοθετησάντων ἢ καὶ φυσιολογίας περὶ ὕδατος η γῆς ἢ τῶν ἀπ᾿ αὐτῆς καρπῶν δοκούντων περιέχειν, δῆλον ὅτι οἱ τὸ θεῖον ἐξητασμένως σέβειν θέλοντες εὔλογόν τι πράττοιεν, μὴ μεταλαμβάνοντες τῶν δημοτελῶν ἑορτῶν. „ἑορτὴ“ γὰρ, ὥς φησι τὶς καὶ τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν σοφῶν καλῶς λέγων. „οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἐστὶν ἢ τὸ τὰ δέοντα πράττειν“· καὶ ἑορτάζει γε κατὰ ἀλήθειαν ὁ „τὰ δέοντα“ πράττων, ἀεὶ εὐχόμενος, διὰ παντὸς θύων τὰς ἀναιμάκτους ἐν ταῖς πρὸς τὸ θεῖον εὐχαῖς θυσίας. διὸ καὶ μεγαλοφυέστατά μοι δοκεῖ παρὰ τῷ Παύλῳ εἰρῆσθαι τό· „ἡμέρας παρατηρεῖσθε καὶ μῆνας καὶ καιροὺς καὶ ἐνιαυτούς; φοβοῦμαι ὑμᾶς μή πως εἰκῇ κεκοπίακα εἰς ὑμᾶς.“
pass_a_gloss: Let us see (ἴδωμεν) also the next things said by Celsus about God (θεός), and how he urges (προτρέπει) us to the use (χρῆσις) of things which in truth are idol-offerings (εἰδωλόθυτα) or, so to name them, demon-offerings (δαιμονιόθυτα), but which he would call, not knowing (μὴ εἰδώς) what is truly sacred (ἱερόν) and what sort the sacrifices (θυσίαι) with Him are, sacred-offerings (ἱερόθυτα). His words: 'But God is common (κοινός) to all, good (ἀγαθός), needing nothing (ἀπροσδεής), outside envy (ἔξω φθόνου); what then prevents those most consecrated (καθωσιωμένους) to him from partaking (μεταλαμβάνειν) also of the public festivals (δημοτελεῖς ἑορταί)?' I do not know what he imagined (φαντασθείς) in thinking it follows (ἀκολουθεῖν) from God's being good, needless and envy-free that the consecrated partake of public festivals. And I say: it would follow, if it were demonstrated (ἀπεδείκνυτο) that the public festivals have nothing erroneous (ἐσφαλμένον) and were legislated (ἐνομοθετήθησαν) from contemplation (θεωρία) of God as consequent on service (θεραπεία) and piety (εὐσέβεια) toward Him. But if the festivals, public as far as the name (μέχρι ὀνόματος), have no demonstrative account (λόγος ἀποδεικτικός) as fitting the service of the divine (τὸ θεῖον), but are refuted as fabrications (ἀναπλάσματα) of those who legislated them however it chanced on account of human histories (ἱστορίαι ἀνθρωπικαί), or seeming to contain natural philosophy (φυσιολογία) about water or earth or its fruits, clearly those wishing to worship (σέβειν) the divine with examination (ἐξητασμένως) would do something reasonable (εὔλογον) in not partaking. For 'a festival (ἑορτή)', as one of the Greek wise men (σοφοί) says well, 'is nothing other than doing the needful things (τὰ δέοντα)'; and he truly keeps festival (ἑορτάζει) who does 'the needful', always praying (εὐχόμενος), continually sacrificing (θύων) the bloodless (ἀναίμακτοι) sacrifices in prayers to the divine. Therefore most magnanimously (μεγαλοφυέστατα) said by Paul: 'Days you observe (παρατηρεῖσθε) and months and seasons and years? I fear for you lest somehow I have toiled (κεκοπίακα) for you in vain (εἰκῇ).'
pass_b_english: Let us look also at what Celsus says next about God, and at how he urges us to make use of what are in truth things sacrificed to idols, or, if I may so call them, things sacrificed to demons, though he himself, since he does not know what is truly sacred or what kind of sacrifices are offered to God, would call them “sacred offerings.” What he says is this: “God at any rate is common to all, good, in need of nothing, and free from envy. What then prevents those who are most devoted to Him from taking part in the public festivals as well?”

I do not know what notion led him to think that it follows from God’s being good, in need of nothing, and free from envy, that those devoted to Him should take part in the public festivals. And I say that it would indeed follow from God’s being good, in need of nothing, and free from envy, that they should take part in the public festivals themselves, if it were proved that the public festivals have nothing amiss in them and were instituted from the contemplation of God as fitting for His service and for piety toward Him. If, however, the public festivals, which are festivals in name only, have no reasoned proof that they suit the service of the divine, but are shown to be fictions of men who instituted them haphazardly on account of certain human stories, or fictions that seem to contain natural lore about water or earth or the fruits the earth bears, then plainly those who wish to worship the divine with careful judgment would be acting reasonably in not taking part in the public festivals.

For “a festival,” as one of the Greek wise men well says, “is nothing other than doing what one ought” (Thucydides 1.70). And he truly keeps festival who does “what he ought,” praying always (1 Thessalonians 5:17), and continually offering the bloodless sacrifices in his prayers to the divine. That is why Paul’s words seem to me most lofty: “Do you observe days and months and seasons and years? I fear for you, that I may somehow have labored over you in vain” (Galatians 4:10–11).

choices.choice: Celsus’s quoted words are in double quotation marks. ἱερόθυτα (‘sacred offerings’) is the pagan term Origen says Celsus would use; Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians 10:28 in some manuscripts, not cited inline as no quotation is made. μέχρι ὀνόματος stands between δημοτελεῖς and ἑορταί and qualifies ‘festivals’: they are festivals in name only, which sets up the definition of a true festival that follows. ὅπως ποτὲ ἔτυχε = ‘haphazardly’, ‘in whatever random way’. The clause beginning ἢ καὶ φυσιολογίας ... δοκούντων περιέχειν is loosely built; δοκούντων is taken as ‘fictions that seem to contain’, parallel to the ‘human stories’ clause. ‘As one of the Greek wise men well says’: the saying matches Thucydides 1.70.8 (the Corinthians on the Athenians, μήτε ἑορτὴν ἄλλο τι ἡγεῖσθαι ἢ τὸ τὰ δέοντα πρᾶξαι); Origen does not name the author and reads the line ethically. ‘Praying always’ (ἀεὶ εὐχόμενος) is cited as an allusion to 1 Thessalonians 5:17 (ἀδιαλείπτως προσεύχεσθε); verbal match is thematic, not exact. Galatians 4:10 is rendered as a question, following the Greek question mark in the edition.
Celsus's 'devoted to him' capitalised to 'Him' (the supreme God, consistent with Origen's reply)
'contain nothing in error, but were laid down' to 'have nothing amiss in them and were instituted' (μὲν ... δέ joins two conditions; it is not a contrast)
'these festivals, public in name only' to 'the public festivals, which are festivals in name only' (μέχρι ὀνόματος qualifies ἑορταί, not δημοτελεῖς)
'have no account that proves them suited' to 'have no reasoned proof that they suit' (λόγος ἀποδεικτικός)
'as chance would have it' (English idiom for 'by coincidence', wrong sense) to 'haphazardly' (ὅπως ποτὲ ἔτυχε)
'Paul's words are spoken with the greatest nobility' (stiff) to 'Paul's words seem to me most lofty' (keeps μοι δοκεῖ)
Galatians 4:10 turned from exclamation into a question to match the Greek question mark; note updated
Thucydides 1.70.8 and Galatians 4:10–11 checked; 1 Thessalonians 5:17 kept as allusion
